source.title_on_document: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on innovation: Evidence from software products

supplement.where: Online Supporting Information section of the Wiley article (p. 35: 'Additional supporting information can be found online in the Supporting Information section at the end of this article'). Appendices A-D are in this PDF.
supplement.holds: S1 summary statistics (Table S1.4 for the novelty analyses); S2 construction of the LSI, TF-IDF, and semantic-embedding similarity scores and the text neutralization; S3-S15 robustness checks (SDID, classical DiD, trends, AI-detection of source code, alternative fixed effects).

paper_design_summary: The authors compare Firefox browser add-on activity from June 2022 to May 2023 with the same calendar months one year earlier, before and after ChatGPT's release in November 2022 (a panel-differences design with category-by-period and month fixed effects). Outcomes are counts of new add-ons and updates, the number of categories new add-ons span, user ratings, and the LSI textual similarity of new add-on descriptions to earlier add-ons. No person is assigned to AI and individual AI use is not observed; a survey of 33 developers adds self-reported mechanism evidence.

participants.who: Corpus of Firefox add-ons (software products) by third-party developers, new and existing: initial data set of 31,265 add-ons (p. 13, Section 4.2). Category-level panel of 15 categories x 12 months x 2 periods = 360 category-months (p. 17, fn. 19); add-on-level update panel of 1,745 add-ons x 12 x 2 = 41,880 add-on-months (p. 14, Section 4.3). outcomes.name: LSI similarity score of new add-on descriptions to previous add-ons (inverse novelty)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Latent Semantic Indexing similarity of the descriptions of newly introduced add-ons to previously introduced add-ons, averaged to the category-month; higher = more similar = less novel, so the sign is reversed relative to novelty. Variant on 'neutralized' description text adjusted for GAI writing style (Table 6, col. 3). Paper says results hold with TF-IDF scores and semantic embeddings (p. 25, fn. 24; Supporting Information S2, not read).

studies.label: Exploratory survey of 33 Firefox add-on developers

assignment.unit: individual | team | class | session | within_person_order | other

participants.exclusions: Of 37 initial developer responses, 4 were excluded for failing an attention-check question, leaving 33 analyzed developers (p. 44, Appendix D.1).
participants.who: Firefox add-on developers answering an online survey on their experiences with and perceptions of GAI; supplemented by qualitative developer interviews.
participants.quote: we also collected primary data through a survey of 33 Firefox add-on developers

ai_tool.name_model: GAI tools in general (ChatGPT, Claude mentioned by respondents)
ai_tool.how_used: Self-reported use for ideation and coding; no AI condition is assigned.

task.description: Self-report questionnaire on ideation, implementation, timelines, and competition; no creative output is scored.

eligibility.reason: Neither study randomly assigns people to generative-AI assistance, so criterion 1 is not_met and core remains no. S1 is an observational panel-differences analysis comparing Firefox add-on outputs before and after ChatGPT's release with the same calendar months in the prior year (pp. 15-18, Sections 4.4-4.5). Its distinct-person analysis count is not reported: the 360 category-months and 41,880 add-on-months count panel observations, not people, so criterion 2 is unclear for S1 and at paper level (p. 14, Section 4.3; p. 17, footnote 19). S1 meets criterion 3 through computed novelty scores on actual add-on descriptions (pp. 25-26, Section 5.5 and Table 6). S2 analyzed 33 developers after 4 attention-check exclusions from 37 initial responses, so criterion 2 is not_met for S2; it measures self-reports and has no scored creative output (pp. 43-44, Appendix D and D.1). The paper remains observational context.

one_line_finding: After ChatGPT's release, new Firefox add-ons rose about 34.4 percent (log-OLS 0.2950, p = .0003; p. 19, Table 2) and spanned more categories (0.0568, p = .0241), but their description similarity to earlier add-ons did not fall (LSI 0.0070, p = .1108; neutralized text 0.0069, p = .0416; p. 25, Table 6), while updates to existing add-ons fell about 20.3 percent (Poisson -0.2263; p. 24, Table 5).
